title: A Minaret Lost in the Mountains
text: Far from any town, in a deep river valley about 215 km east of Herat, the Ghurid Sultan Ghiyas-od-din raised a 65-metre minaret of fired brick in 1194. Geometric relief and a Kufic inscription in turquoise tiles cover it completely. It probably marks the lost Ghurid summer capital of Firuzkuh, and its design influenced Delhi's Qutb Minar.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Minaret and Archaeological Remains of Jam

title: Timur's White Palace at Kesh
place: Ak-Sarai Palace, Shakhrisyabz, Kashkadarya Region, Uzbekistan
text: Construction of the Ak-Sarai Palace in Shakhrisyabz began in 1380, the year after Timur conquered Khorezm. Khorezm's artisans were deported to work on it and to create its rich decoration. Today only the foundations of its immense gate survive, yet UNESCO judges that none of Samarkand's many Timurid monuments can rival it.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic Centre of Shakhrisyabz

title: A Market Street Built in Twenty Days
text: On September 8, 1404, Ruy Gonzalez de Clavijo, envoy of King Henry III of Castile, reached Samarkand and was greeted by six elephants carrying wooden castles. He then watched Timur order a covered street of shops, with stone benches and fountains, cut straight through the city. Crews worked day and night and finished it in twenty days, though evicted homeowners had good cause to complain.

source.name: Origins (Ohio State University): A Castilian in Samarkand, 1404

source2.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): Clavijo's Embassy to Tamerlane

title: A Taoist Master Winters in Samarkand
text: Summoned by Genghis Khan, the elderly Taoist monk Changchun reached Samarkand in December 1221. His disciple's diary describes canals bringing river water to every house, but notes that only a quarter of the city's families remained after the Mongol conquest. Changchun wintered in the Sultan's palace, saw elephants from India, and compared notes on a solar eclipse with a local astronomer.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): The Travels of Ch'ang Ch'un to the West, 1220-1223

title: A Friar in a Market Town of Many Faiths
place: Kayalyk (Cailac), near Koylyk, Zhetysu Region, Kazakhstan
text: Heading for the Mongol court in 1253, the Flemish friar William of Rubruck rested twelve days at Cailac, a big market town frequented by many traders. He entered its 'idol temples', whose priests shaved their heads and wore saffron robes. Leaving town, his party found a village entirely of Nestorian Christians and sang the Salve Regina in their church, overjoyed to see one after so long.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): William of Rubruck's account of the Mongols

title: A Silk Coat Fit for a Prince
text: In the 700s a five-colour silk was woven with paired ducks inside pearl roundels, hallmarks of the precious silks of Sogdia. It was made into a child's coat lined with Chinese floral damask, presumably for a Tibetan prince. The coat looks so pristine that it may never have been worn; it might have served as a diplomatic gift or even as currency.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Child's Coat with Ducks in Pearl Medallions

title: A Pharmacy Jar with a Proverb
text: This albarello, a jar designed to hold ointments and drugs for pharmacists, was made in Samarkand in the 900s, under the Samanid dynasty. Such jars usually carried flowers or geometric patterns, but this one bears elegant Arabic writing in Eastern Kufic script: 'Modesty comes from faith, and faith comes from Paradise,' a saying attributed to the Prophet Muhammad.

source.name: Cleveland Museum of Art: Albarello Jar with an Aphorism

title: Gawharshad's Tiled Mosque in Herat
text: Gawharshad, wife of the Timurid ruler Shahrukh, was a great builder. Her mosque in Herat, raised between 1417 and 1438 beside an open-air prayer ground north of the city walls, had a courtyard 116 by 64 metres, polychrome tiles everywhere and marble-clad minarets with exquisite calligraphy. Her mausoleum of 1432, crowned by a ribbed blue-tiled dome, still stands.

source.name: Leiden University, Iran-Turan project: Gawharshad Complex, Herat

title: The Mosque with Tile Dragons
place: Anau, near Ashgabat, Ahal Region, Turkmenistan
text: In 1455–1456 a Timurid shrine for Shaykh Jamal al-Din rose on a hill over Anau's old city wall, near today's Ashgabat. Its mosque portal was famous for a tile mosaic of a pair of dragons, with panels fastened by lead pins, and its windows glowed with coloured glass. An earthquake destroyed it in 1948, but scholar Galina Pugachenkova had recorded the site in 1947.

source.name: Leiden University, Iran-Turan project: Shrine of Shaykh Jamal al-Din (1455-1456)

title: The Oldest Madrasa on the Registan
text: Built in 1417–1420, Ulugh Beg's madrasa, an Islamic religious school, is the oldest surviving monument on Samarkand's Registan Square. Its later story is dramatic: photographs from 1901 show its northern and southern facades as piles of rubble, and its whole courtyard had to be rebuilt. In 1932 an engineer from Moscow straightened a leaning minaret on the square's facade.

source.name: Leiden University, Iran-Turan project: The Registan Square (15th-17th century)

source2.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): Samarkand, Ulugh Beg's Observatory

title: A Mother Builds a Tomb for Her Daughter
text: In 1372 Turkan Aqa built a mausoleum at Samarkand's Shah-i Zinda shrine for her daughter Shad-i Mulk Aqa, Timur's niece, and she may be buried there too. Its deeply carved terracotta tiles resemble Chinese lacquerware, hinting at influence from objects brought from China. Unusually, the tomb's inner dome still keeps its tiles, though so many domes there collapsed within a century or so.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington), Daniel C. Waugh: Samarkand, Shah-i-Zinde

title: Giant Melons and Fist-Sized Pomegranates
text: Yelü Chucai, an official marching west with Genghis Khan's army in 1219, filled his notes with fruit. Khujand's pomegranates were as large as two fists and were squeezed into a thirst-slaking drink. In the town of Ba-p'u, he wrote, watermelons weighed fifty pounds, so a donkey could carry only two, while Samarkand's melons were as large as a horse's head.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): Ye-lü Ch'u-ts'ai's account of Central Asia (Si Yu Lu)

title: A Silk Road City in the Clouds
text: Between the 6th and 11th centuries, Tugunbulak flourished 2,000 to 2,200 metres up in the mountains of southeastern Uzbekistan. Drone-mounted lidar has revealed its plazas, fortifications, roads and homes across 120 hectares, making it one of the largest highland cities of its time. Its fortress, with rammed-earth walls three metres thick, may have been a factory where smiths turned iron ore into steel.

source.name: Washington University in St. Louis, Arts & Sciences: High-res lidar exposes large, high-elevation cities along Asia's Silk Roads

source2.name: Nature (Frachetti et al. 2024): Large-scale medieval urbanism traced by UAV-lidar in highland Central Asia

title: A Coin Stamped 'Turk-Kagan'
text: A small bronze coin from the late 6th or early 7th century, found at an ancient site near Tashkent, is stamped 'Turk-Kagan' in the Sogdian language. Archaeologist Gaybulla Babayarov argues it is the oldest known reference to Turkic identity. Probably minted in the Western Gokturk Khaganate, it suggests these supposedly purely nomadic rulers had towns, a ruling elite and money.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine (Archaeological Institute of America): Bronze Coin May Contain Earliest Known Usage of the Word 'Turk'

title: A Papal Envoy Crosses Ruined Lands
place: Lower Syr Darya steppe, Kyzylorda Region, Kazakhstan
text: Riding to the Mongol court in 1246, the papal envoy John of Plano Carpini crossed steppe where human skulls and bones lay scattered on the ground like cattle dung. Next came the land of Turkic-speaking Muslims, with 'innumerable ruined cities' along a great river, among them Ianckint, Barchin and Ornas. Their sultan, he heard, had been killed by the Mongols with all his family.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): John of Pian de Carpine's journey

title: The Astronomer King Loses His Head
text: Ulugh Beg, Timur's scholarly grandson, governed Samarkand for decades and became supreme ruler when his father Shahrukh died in 1447. He survived only two years on his own before being overthrown and beheaded in 1449. Some scholars he had supported then left Samarkand for more stable capitals such as Istanbul, and his observatory was destroyed within a few generations. He lies at Timur's feet in the Gur-i Amir.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): Samarkand, Ulugh Beg's Observatory
